chunks: "Think of it as a very fast stopwatch with a laser. A controller fires a laser diode with a short pulse, a few nanoseconds long, and at the same moment starts a timer.
The light travels to the target, scatters off it, and a small fraction comes back through the receive lens onto a detector, usually an avalanche photodiode.
That detector produces a tiny current, maybe a microamp at 100 meters, which a transimpedance amplifier turns into a voltage.
A comparator, or a fast ADC, detects when the pulse arrives and a time-to-digital converter stops the timer.
The range is the speed of light times the time difference, divided by two, because the light went out and back.
200 nanoseconds is 30 meters, and every nanosecond is 15 centimeters.
The controller also knows which direction the laser was pointing, from the scanner's angle, so each measurement becomes an x, y, z point.

The hard part is precision: to get a centimeter you need around 70 picoseconds of timing accuracy, and the return amplitude varies by a thousand, so a fixed threshold makes bright targets look closer than dim ones, called walk error.
Designers fix that with constant-fraction discrimination or by digitizing the waveform.
Range is limited by the laser power, which is capped by eye safety, the receiver's sensitivity, and sunlight noise."
